title: Solids, Liquids and Gases
blurb: Density and pressure formulas are asked almost every session, and there is nearly always a particle-model explanation worth several marks.
formulas: p₁ ÷ T₁ = p₂ ÷ T₂  (T in kelvin)

items.q: State the formula linking density, mass and volume.
a: density = mass ÷ volume
(ρ = m ÷ V)
items.tip: Watch the units: 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³. Water is 1.0 g/cm³ or 1000 kg/m³.

items.q: State the formula linking pressure, force and area.
a: pressure = force ÷ area
(p = F ÷ A)
items.tip: The force must be perpendicular to the surface. Area in m² gives pressure in pascals.

items.q: State the formula linking pressure difference, height, density and gravitational field strength.
a: pressure difference = height × density × gravitational field strength
(p = h × ρ × g)
items.tip: The height is the depth below the surface, measured vertically. The shape or width of the container makes no difference.

items.q: Describe the arrangement and motion of the particles in a solid, a liquid and a gas.
a: Solid: particles are close together in a regular, fixed pattern and vibrate about fixed positions;
Liquid: particles are still close together but irregularly arranged, and can move past one another randomly;
Gas: particles are far apart, randomly arranged, and move quickly in all directions (random motion);
the particles have more kinetic energy as you go from solid to liquid to gas.
items.tip: Two things are always wanted: the arrangement (how they are positioned) and the motion (how they move). Answer both explicitly.

items.q: Explain, using the particle model, why the pressure of a gas increases when its temperature increases (at constant volume).
a: The particles gain kinetic energy and move faster;
so they collide with the walls of the container more frequently;
and each collision exerts a greater force (bigger change in momentum);
the force on a given area increases, so the pressure increases.
items.tip: Both reasons are needed - more frequent collisions AND harder collisions. Never say the particles themselves expand.

items.q: Explain, using the particle model, why the pressure of a gas increases when its volume decreases.
items.rx: volume of the (gas|air)|gas is compressed|syringe|(pressure|volume) of the gas
a: The particles have a smaller space, so they hit the walls more often (more collisions per second);
the average speed of the particles is unchanged because the temperature is constant;
so the force per unit area, and therefore the pressure, increases (p₁V₁ = p₂V₂).

items.q: Use the graph to determine the value of absolute zero / convert between °C and K.
a: Absolute zero is −273 °C, which is 0 K;
it is the lowest possible temperature, at which the particles have no (minimum) kinetic energy;
to convert, add 273 to a Celsius temperature to get kelvin.
items.tip: Extrapolate the pressure–temperature line backwards until it crosses the temperature axis at zero pressure - that intercept is absolute zero.

items.q: Describe how the student should accurately measure the mass and the volume of the object to find its density.
a: Mass: use a (top-pan) balance, zero it first, and for a liquid weigh the empty container then the container plus liquid and subtract;
Volume of a regular solid: measure the dimensions with a ruler or vernier calipers and multiply;
Volume of an irregular solid: lower it into a measuring cylinder of water and record the increase in level (or use a displacement can and catch the water);
calculate density = mass ÷ volume;
repeat the measurements and take a mean.
items.tip: For the measuring-cylinder reading, mention reading at eye level from the bottom of the meniscus - it is often worth a mark.

items.q: Describe what happens to the particles when a substance melts, boils or evaporates.
a: Energy supplied increases the (potential) energy of the particles and weakens or breaks the bonds between them;
during a change of state the temperature stays constant because the energy goes into breaking bonds, not into speeding the particles up;
evaporation happens only at the surface, at any temperature, when the fastest particles escape; boiling happens throughout the liquid at a fixed temperature;
as the fastest particles leave, the average kinetic energy of those remaining falls, so the liquid cools.
items.tip: The cooling effect of evaporation is a favourite. The key phrase is 'the most energetic particles escape'.
